pages.title: The DC shunt motor
pages.for: Work that needs a steady speed as the load changes. The field sits across the supply, so its flux holds steady. Under load the speed dips only a little.
pages.rule:
Field across the supply, so the flux holds steady.
If = V ÷ Rf
V = E + Ia Ra
Line current = Ia + If
Speed goes with E ÷ flux.
Torque goes with flux × Ia.
Speed regulation = (no-load − full-load speed) ÷ full-load speed.

Nearly constant speed. Regulation is quoted at about 5 to 10%, sometimes 10 to 20%. Use the maker's figure.
Starting torque is lower than a series motor's.
Base speed is the nameplate speed at full field and full armature volts.
Below base speed, lower the armature volts. Above it, weaken the field.
Reverse it: swap the armature or the field leads, not both.

traps.text: More field resistance means more speed, not less. Weakening the field speeds it up.
Lose the field and it can run away on a light load. Make sure loss-of-field protection is fitted.
Start at full field, with the rheostat at its slow-speed position. Start through the starter's resistance.
It does not speed back up after a load goes on. It usually settles a little slower. That fall is its speed regulation.
Isolate, lock off and prove dead. Then megger to frame, measure field and armature resistance, and check the brushes and commutator.

pages.where: Pumps, fans, blowers, conveyors, machine tools and printing: where the speed must hold near its setting.

pages.name: Do you still have it?
pages.task: A DC motor is switched straight onto its supply. Before it starts to turn, what sets the current it draws?
pages.answer: Only the resistance of its armature circuit
pages.alt: A motor makes back-emf only as it turns, so at standstill there is none. Only the resistance limits the current. Take a motor with a 0.07 Ω armature on 600 V. Switched straight on, it would take 600 ÷ 0.07 = 8571 A. That is why it starts through a starter.
options: Its back-emf, which opposes the supply
Only the resistance of its armature circuit
The inductance of its windings, as on AC
pages.html: A motor makes back-emf only as it turns, so at standstill there is none. Only the resistance limits the current. Take a motor with a 0.07 Ω armature on 600 V. Switched straight on, it would take 600 ÷ 0.07 = 8571 A. That is why it starts through a starter.

pages.name: How it works
pages.text:
The shunt field winding is wired across the supply, beside the armature. So its current and its flux stay steady whatever the load.

Load the motor and it slows a little. Its back-emf falls, so more armature current flows. More current gives more torque. It settles where the torque matches the load, a little slower than before.

Unlike a series motor's field, this one does not follow the load. So the speed hardly moves.
pages.alt: DC supply 600 V line current armature current field current field rheostat shunt field armature turning back-emf

pages.name: Load it, weaken the field
pages.text: From no load to rated load the field current stays at 7.5 A. The back-emf falls from 598.8 to 575.8 V. The armature current rises from 17.3 to 345.5 A. The speed dips only from 2080 to 2000 rpm. Add 20 Ω to the field and its current falls to 6.0 A. At rated load it then runs at 2474 rpm on 431.9 A, above rated. With no load it reaches about 2600 rpm, past the example limit. Open the field on a light load and it runs away.
pages.alt: Then add field resistance. Then open the field. Assume this 600 V motor: 0.07 Ω armature and 80 Ω field. At rated load it runs at 2000 rpm and draws 353 A from the supply. The supply covers the back-emf and the armature drop: V = E + Ia Ra. Back-emf goes with flux × speed. Torque goes with flux × Ia. The no-load current and the 2500 rpm limit are examples. V = 600 V rheostat shunt field 80 Ω flux If 7.5 A residual magnetism only Ia armature Ra 0.07 Ω back-emf E Ia × Ra 24.2 V Back-emf bar: 0 to 600 V. Drop bar: 0 to 60 V, drawn 10 times bigger. Field open: no figures here.
pages.html:
Then add field resistance. Then open the field.

Assume this 600 V motor: 0.07 Ω armature and 80 Ω field. At rated load it runs at 2000 rpm and draws 353 A from the supply. The supply covers the back-emf and the armature drop: V = E + Ia Ra. Back-emf goes with flux × speed. Torque goes with flux × Ia. The no-load current and the 2500 rpm limit are examples.

Armature current345.5 A
Back-emf575.8 V
Speed2000 rpm

At 100% load the field still takes 7.5 A, so the flux holds. The back-emf has fallen to 575.8 V, letting 345.5 A through the armature. The speed has dipped only to 2000 rpm.

Worked from the rule

Rated load, full field: If = 600 ÷ 80 = 7.5 A. Ia = 353 − 7.5 = 345.5 A. Drop = 345.5 × 0.07 = 24.2 V. E = 600 − 24.2 = 575.8 V. Speed 2000 rpm.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: A shunt motor is driving a steady load. You turn the field rheostat to add resistance. What does the speed do?
pages.alt: Less field current means less flux. The armature must spin faster to make the back-emf it needs. So the speed rises. On the picture, 20 Ω takes the rated-load speed from 2000 to 2474 rpm. That is called field weakening.
pages.html: Less field current means less flux. The armature must spin faster to make the back-emf it needs. So the speed rises. On the picture, 20 Ω takes the rated-load speed from 2000 to 2474 rpm. That is called field weakening.

pages.name: How it behaves
pages.text:
Speed: Nearly constant. Its speed regulation is (no-load − full-load speed) ÷ full-load speed. Here (2080 − 2000) ÷ 2000 = 4.0%. Quoted figures are about 5 to 10%, sometimes 10 to 20%. Use the maker's.

Starting torque: Lower than a series motor's. Typically about 250%, set by the starter.

Speed control: Base speed is the nameplate speed at full field and full armature volts. Below it, lower the armature volts. Above it, weaken the field.

Reversing: Swap the armature or the field leads, not both.
pages.alt: 0 1000 2000 3000 0 20 40 60 80 100 Speed, rpm Load, % of rated torque 2080 rpm at no load 2000 rpm at rated load sketch from the simplified rule

pages.name: Where it is used
pages.text:
Used for: Pumps, fans, blowers, conveyors, machine tools and printing. Anywhere the speed must hold steady as the load changes.

Unloaded: Safe running light at full field, as long as the field stays connected. A series motor would run away.

Drive: It pairs well with a thyristor drive, which sets the armature voltage. Many plants have moved to AC motors on VSDs.

Limits: Brushes and commutator need regular care. A weakened field can overspeed at light load. Never pass the nameplate's maximum safe speed.
pages.alt: thyristor drive armature volts shunt motor conveyor

pages.name: Faults and tests
pages.text:
Safety first: Isolate, lock off and prove dead before you touch it.

Field open: On a light load it can run away. Loss-of-field protection guards against it.

Starting: Start at full field, with the rheostat at its slow-speed position.

Starter: A three-point starter's no-volt coil carries the field current. Lose the supply or the field and its handle drops to off.

Sparking: Worn brushes, a rough commutator or an armature fault.

Tests: Megger the windings to frame. Measure the armature and field resistance. An open field reads open circuit.
pages.alt: isolator: open locked off and tagged megger windings frame ohmmeter field winding brushes commutator

pages.name: Find the fault
pages.task: A shunt motor drives a conveyor that is running almost empty. It has run at a steady speed for years. Today it races until its protection trips. What is the most likely fault?
pages.answer: The shunt field circuit has gone open
pages.alt: With the field open, only residual magnetism is left. The armature must spin far faster to make its back-emf. On a light load it runs away. Isolate and prove dead. Then test the field winding, its rheostat and its connections for an open circuit.
options: The belt came off, so it lost its load
The shunt field circuit has gone open
pages.html: With the field open, only residual magnetism is left. The armature must spin far faster to make its back-emf. On a light load it runs away. Isolate and prove dead. Then test the field winding, its rheostat and its connections for an open circuit.
